q: What is a sol?
a: A sol is one Martian day. The mission counts its days in sols from landing: sol 1 is landing day, and Opportunity's last message came on sol 5111, 10 June 2018.

q: Why does hematite matter?
a: Hematite is an iron-rich mineral that typically forms in water. Meridiani Planum shows signs of coarse-grained hematite, which is why it is also called the 'Hematite Site', and why the rover was sent there.

q: How long was it supposed to last?
a: It was designed for 90 Martian days and about 1,000 metres of driving. It explored for more than 14 years and drove more than 45 kilometres.

q: Why does jarosite point to acidic water?
a: The Mössbauer spectrometer found jarosite in the outcrop. The mission team said jarosite may point to the rock's wet history having been in an acidic lake or an acidic hot springs environment.

q: What are the 'blueberries'?
a: Small round grains, called spherules, scattered in and on the rock. Comparing areas with and without them, and looking at them with Pancam, showed they contain hematite, which NASA says was deposited in water.

q: Does this mean there was life?
a: No. The rocks show that liquid water was once there, and that it was acidic. They do not show that anything lived there.

q: How deep was it stuck?
a: The wheels sank more than 10 centimetres, to the depth of the wheel hubs, in a sand ripple about a third of a metre tall and 2.5 metres wide.

q: How do we know it barely moved?
a: The traverse table has 326 position records between sols 447 and 484. Between the first and the last of them, the rover moved only about 1.6 metres.

q: Why is this spot brighter on the trail?
a: On this stage every position record is drawn as a faint point of light. Where many records pile up in one place, as they do at Purgatory, the light adds up. The glow is a way of drawing the data, not something seen on Mars.

q: What is HiRISE?
a: A camera on NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter. It took the orbital picture of Victoria crater shown at this stop, which gives its size as about 800 metres across.

q: Why were the layers exciting?
a: The crater wall exposed layers of rock. Steve Squyres said that those layers, if the rover could get to them, would tell new stories about the environmental conditions long ago.

q: How far had it driven by then?
a: More than 9.2 kilometres since landing, most of it on the 21-month journey from Endurance crater.

q: How big is Endeavour?
a: About 22 kilometres in diameter, more than 25 times wider than Victoria crater.

q: Why do clay minerals matter?
a: Clays typically form in wet environments that are not harshly acidic. Finding them would mean Mars once had gentler water than the acidic water seen at Eagle crater.

q: How long did the drive take?
a: Nearly three years and about 21 kilometres, from the time Opportunity left Victoria crater to its arrival at Spirit Point on 9 August 2011.

q: What does the Rock Abrasion Tool do?
a: It sits on the turret at the end of the robotic arm. Its rotating, grinding teeth gnaw into the surface of a rock so the other instruments can study what is inside.

q: Could anything have lived there?
a: Steve Squyres said this water would have provided more favourable conditions for biology than any other wet environment recorded in rocks Opportunity had seen. That describes conditions; it is not evidence that anything lived there.

q: Why does the photo look so strange?
a: It is a false-colour Pancam image: its colours are chosen to make different materials stand out, not to match what your eye would see. The area shown is about 70 centimetres across.

q: Why couldn't it recharge?
a: Opportunity ran on solar power. A dust storm that covered the planet blanketed the rover's location in June 2018 and blocked the sunlight.

q: Why is the last photo almost black?
a: Dust blocked the Sun, the white specks are camera noise, and the bottom is blank because the transmission was cut off.

q: Where is Opportunity now?
a: In Perseverance Valley, on the inner slope of Endeavour crater's western rim, where its route ends on NASA's final traverse map. It has been inactive since June 2018.

q: How hard did NASA try to reach it?
a: Engineers sent more than 1,000 recovery commands over eight months. The last attempt was on 12 February 2019, and NASA ended the mission on 13 February 2019.

q: Why 45.16 km here and 45.1 km on the trail?
a: 45.16 km is NASA's figure on its final traverse map. The trail on this stage adds up straight lines between 21,089 position records, which comes to 45.1 km. Different ways of measuring give slightly different totals.

q: Is Opportunity abandoned?
a: It is inactive, but not forgotten. The NASA Space Apps 2026 challenge lists Spirit and Opportunity as twin rovers that operated for years and are now inactive monuments to Mars exploration.
